viewpoints.title: Digital Privacy in the Workplace
viewpoints.script: I want to talk about something that concerns me deeply—workplace monitoring and digital privacy. Many companies today monitor their employees constantly: they track keystrokes, monitor websites visited, log bathroom breaks through card access, and even use AI to analyze email and chat conversations. The argument is usually that this improves productivity and security, but I think it's gone too far. Yes, employers have legitimate security concerns, but the level of surveillance we're accepting is unprecedented. When employees feel constantly watched, it creates anxiety and erodes trust. Studies show that excessive monitoring actually decreases productivity and morale. Workers spend time trying to appear productive rather than actually being productive. Moreover, there's a moral issue here. As an employee, you're a person, not a machine to be optimized. You deserve privacy and dignity at work. I'm not arguing against all monitoring—reasonable security measures are necessary. But there's a middle ground between trusting employees completely and treating them like suspects. Companies that have implemented less invasive monitoring policies actually report higher employee satisfaction and retention. So my position is this: employers should use targeted monitoring only where necessary for genuine security reasons, not blanket surveillance of everything everyone does. Trust and respect for employee privacy create better workplaces.

UBI would be simpler and less wasteful. Second, the economic stimulus of putting money in people's hands is significant. When people have financial security, they spend more, which supports businesses and creates jobs. Third, UBI addresses real problems: poverty, economic instability, and lack of opportunity. We've seen pilot projects in Kenya, Finland, and Canada that show positive outcomes. In Kenya, UBI increased business formation by 32 percent. In Finland, participants reported better mental health and less anxiety. Some worry it will make people lazy, but that's not supported by evidence. People want purpose and contribution, not just money. What UBI does is give them the freedom to pursue education, care for family, or start businesses without desperation. The real question isn't whether we can afford UBI—it's whether we can afford not to implement it. Rising inequality and automation are creating unprecedented challenges.

viewpoints.title: Climate Migration and Urban Planning

This means developing infrastructure and housing in climate-resilient areas, creating economic opportunities for migrants, and managing population flows thoughtfully. Canada and the northern regions of other countries will likely become more desirable as climate conditions shift. Rather than letting this happen chaotically, we should be designing inclusive urban expansion, building climate-resilient communities, and preparing labor markets for population shifts. Some people see climate migration as a negative, but it's inevitable. The real question is whether we manage it responsibly or let it cause humanitarian crises. I'm advocating for proactive planning now. We should be expanding housing, infrastructure, and economic capacity in climate-safe regions. We should also help other countries adapt in place where possible. But denying this reality and refusing to plan is irresponsible.

viewpoints.title: Algorithmic Bias in Hiring Systems
viewpoints.script: Algorithmic bias in hiring is a serious problem that companies are using as a shortcut without taking responsibility for the consequences. Many organizations now use AI systems to screen resumes, assess candidate fit, and predict job performance. These systems seem objective—they're just mathematics, right? Wrong. These algorithms are trained on historical data, which includes decades of human bias. If women were historically excluded from leadership positions, the algorithm learns that pattern and replicates it. If certain demographics were underrepresented in technical roles, the algorithm reinforces that exclusion. Studies have documented this repeatedly. Amazon famously scrapped their hiring algorithm when they discovered it was discriminating against women. Google's recruiting algorithm showed bias against applicants from historically black colleges. These weren't intentional—that's precisely the problem. The systems' creators didn't set out to discriminate; they just trusted that math was unbiased, when in reality, data is never neutral. My argument is this: companies should not deploy algorithmic hiring systems without rigorous bias testing and external auditing. If you use an algorithm to screen candidates, you're making a business decision, and you're responsible for its outcomes. You can't hide behind the algorithm or claim you didn't know it was biased. Moreover, algorithms eliminate human judgment, nuance, and chance. They can't capture potential, resilience, or growth. Some of the most successful employees wouldn't have passed an algorithm. We need a return to more human-centered hiring while using algorithms cautiously and with oversight.

We talk about mental health awareness, but when it comes to actual coverage, it's dramatically underfunded. Most insurance plans cover mental health at lower rates than physical health. If you have a broken arm, insurance covers months of physical therapy. If you have depression or anxiety, you get maybe 10 sessions of therapy a year, and psychologist visits might only be 50 percent covered. This creates barriers. Many people avoid treatment because they can't afford it, and their conditions worsen. The economic impact is massive. Mental health issues cost the economy 51 billion dollars annually in Canada through lost productivity, emergency services, and hospitalizations. Yet we invest a fraction of that in prevention and treatment. Here's what frustrates me most: we have effective treatments. Therapy works. Medication helps. But access is limited by insurance coverage. A person struggling with bipolar disorder shouldn't have to choose between therapy and rent. Insurance companies argue coverage limits are necessary for cost control, but that's shortsighted. When people get mental health treatment early, they use fewer emergency services, work more, and contribute to society. The ROI on mental health coverage is actually positive. I'm advocating for mandatory parity—insurance companies should cover mental health at the same level as physical health. This means removing visit limits, lowering copayments, and covering evidence-based treatments. It's not just compassionate; it's economically smart.
